title: Sleep Training, Without the Dogma
hook: There's no single 'right' way to help a baby sleep. Readiness is usually around 4–6 months, methods range from gradual check-ins to gentler approaches, and consistency matters most.
key_points: Babies generally aren't ready until around 4–6 months, when regular sleep cycles start to develop.
There's a spectrum of methods: graduated check-ins, bedtime fading, and gentler no-cry approaches.
A core idea across methods is putting baby down drowsy but awake so they learn to settle themselves.
Consistency matters more than which method you pick — and safe-sleep rules still apply.
content_html: "Sleep training" sounds like one thing, but it's really a family of approaches, and the AAP is deliberately neutral about which to choose. Readiness usually comes around four to six months, when babies start developing regular sleep cycles — it's not a newborn task. From there, the methods span a spectrum: graduated check-ins (going in to comfort at lengthening intervals), bedtime fading (shifting bedtime to match when your baby actually gets sleepy), and gentler, no-cry approaches.
extra_html: The thread running through all of them, per the AAP, is putting your baby down drowsy but awake so they learn to settle themselves and drift back to sleep after the normal night wakings. No single method is "the right one," and consistency tends to matter more than which brand of advice you follow. Whatever you choose, safe sleep doesn't change: back-sleeping on a firm, flat, bare surface for every sleep. This is general guidance; your pediatrician can help you pick an approach that fits your baby and your family.

related.title: When Good Sleep Suddenly Gets Worse
related.hook: Sleep that was going well can fall apart around growth spurts, teething, travel, or illness. These rough patches are normal, they pass, and a steady routine helps you ride them out.

related.title: A Safe Sleep Space for Baby
related.hook: Pediatric guidance for safer infant sleep is simple: a firm, flat surface with nothing in it — no pillows, blankets, bumpers, or soft toys.

flashcards.prompt: Around what age are babies usually ready for sleep training?

choices.text: Around 4–6 months, when regular sleep cycles begin to develop

flashcards.explanation_html: The AAP ties readiness to babies developing regular sleep cycles, which happens around 4 to 6 months — not in the newborn period.

flashcards.prompt: What technique shows up across most sleep-training approaches?
flashcards.back_html: Putting baby down drowsy but awake, so they learn to fall asleep — and fall back asleep after night wakings — on their own.

flashcards.prompt: What matters most when choosing a sleep-training method?

choices.text: Switching methods every night until one works

flashcards.explanation_html: The AAP doesn't endorse one method; approaches range from graduated check-ins to gentler ones, and consistency matters more than the brand. Safe-sleep rules still apply.
